newsitem.title: USA: Labeling gene crops to stay a European priority.
newsitem.headline: Labeling gene crops to stay a European priority.

text.p: European consumers' resistance to food products made from gene-altered crops mean that efforts to label those products will remain a top policy priority for many countries, a trade official said Thursday.
"Labeling is still in the heat of the debate," Arnold Mergell, chairman of the German Oilseed Crushers Association said in an interview with Reuters Thursday.

Although the European Union approved the use of gene- altered soybeans in food and seed in 1996, several European nations have called for the labeling of all or some products containing genetically-modified crops, Mergell said at a meeting of the National Institute of Oilseed Products.

For example in Austria, the environment minister has called for mandatory labeling of all "genetically modified raw material and feeds," according to an attache report from the U.S. Foreign Agriculture Service.
In addition, many other European nations are considering labeling proposals because of consumer resistance to products containing gene-altered soybeans.
But Mergell contended that labeling gene-altered products is unnecessary because the gene-altered soybeans currently on the market are identical to those that have not been modified.
"Oil from a GM (genetically modified) soya bean is the same as a non-modified," Mergell said.
European consumers are opposed to the use of genetically-modified crops in food products in part because of highly visible publicity campaigns by environmental groups like Greenpeace, Mergell said.
"They (Greenpeace) really spread this mistrust," Mergell said. "So when they (consumers) hear this message from morning to afternoon, they become hesitant."
Others also attested to the success of Greenpeace's efforts to spark consumer opposition to the use of genetically-modified crops.

"It is well-known that German consumers have been very reluctant to accept genetically-modified food products, and that groups such as Greenpeace have seen some success on this issue as a result," a U.S. FAS attache in Germany wrote in a report.

Many European nations are now awaiting further interpretation of the the EU's Novel Foods Regulation, which goes into effect in May. Under the regulation, some gene-altered foods will be subject to labeling, Mergell said.
"The issue right now is novel food interpretation," Mergell said.
